name: Treaty with the Delawares, 1854
aka: Treaty of Washington with the Delaware, May 6, 1854
promises: A reserved part of the Kansas lands kept as the Delawares' permanent home (Article 1).
The ceded 'trust lands' would be surveyed and offered for sale at public auction under the public land laws (Article 2).
All money from those sales, less the costs of survey and sale, paid to the tribe, plus $10,000 for the 'outlet' strip (Article 3).
Money not needed for current wants invested by the President in safe stocks, the principal kept unimpaired (Article 7).
Railroads crossing the reservation would pay just compensation in money for their right of way (Article 12).

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found, and the United States conceded, that it did not sell the 557,955 acres of trust lands at public auction as Article 2 required. It held the United States breached its duty, found the lands worth $2,443,516 against $1,057,898.19 realized, and awarded the $1,385,617.81 difference plus 5 per cent simple interest from 30 April 1857, $9,168,171.13 as of 31 August 1969.

breaches.what: The Commission held in 1959 that the Delaware Outlet, released under Article 3 for $10,000, was worth $617,980 when ceded and that the $10,000 consideration was unconscionable. After the Court of Claims' 1970 decision it entered a final award of $435,873.86, deducting an earlier $150,000 payment on the claim and $22,106.14 in offsets from a gross award of $607,980.

landTaken: The trust lands contained 557,955 acres, exclusive of five townsites including Leavenworth City (Docket 72 findings, 1969).
compensation: The trust lands were sold privately in 1856-57 for $1,057,898.19. The Commission awarded $9,168,171.13 (principal plus interest to August 1969) for the trust lands and a net $435,873.86 in 1971 for the Outlet. Congress appropriated the trust-land award and provided for its distribution by Public Law 92-456 (Delaware Tribal Business Committee v. Weeks).
today: The 1977 Supreme Court case arose from a dispute over who shared in the distribution under Public Law 92-456, which used an eligibility cut-off of 3 October 1972 (Delaware Tribal Business Committee v. Weeks, footnote 13).

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says that after signing the first treaty with the new United States in 1778 its ancestors had to keep giving up their lands and moving west, to Ohio, then Indiana, Missouri and Kansas and at last Indian Territory, and that its people understood many early land sales as something closer to leases.

The Nation's About Us page counts one treaty of its own with the United States, the 1778 treaty, the first any Indigenous nation made with it, and traces its descent to the Cape Girardeau Spanish Land Grant Area.

plain.promised: A permanent home in Kansas, and sale of the ceded trust lands at public auction with all the money, less costs, paid to the tribe, plus $10,000 for the Outlet strip.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1969, and the United States conceded, that it did not sell the 557,955 acres at public auction. In 1959 it held the $10,000 for the Outlet unconscionable.
plain.today: The Commission awarded $9,168,171.13 for the trust lands and a net $435,873.86 for the Outlet. Congress appropriated the trust-land award; who shared in it reached the Supreme Court in 1977. Payment of the Outlet award has not been traced.

openQuestions: The Commission's reasoning on the Outlet (that the $10,000 consideration was unconscionable, as the tribe alleged) was not read in the opinion itself; only the 1971 final award was opened.
The Delaware Tribe of Indians (delawaretribe.org) and the Delaware Nation pages checked carry no history of this treaty; a nation statement is still wanted.
Whether railroads paid for rights of way under Article 12 was not researched; the 1860 and 1866 Delaware treaties (railroad sales) are separate queue entries.
The holding of Delaware Tribal Business Committee v. Weeks on the distribution dispute was not read in full.

Audit 2026-11-08: the Outlet breach now cites the 1959 interlocutory order, which held the $10,000 consideration unconscionable for land worth $617,980 (figure as restated in the 1971 opinion; the 1959 scan prints it variously), so the first open question is answered. The Weeks citation now points to Cornell LII, where the quote was confirmed; the FindLaw page blocks automated readers. Docket 72 figures and the United States' concession held.
